subject: Banking
title: The Savings and Loan Crisis
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Savings and Loan Crisis usable.

hook.text: In the 1980s, over 1,000 US savings and loan banks collapsed. The government bailout cost taxpayers $132 billion.

buildup.text: S&Ls were small banks that took savings and made home loans.

discovery.text: When real estate prices fell, the risky loans went bad. S&Ls had no reserves. The government had to absorb the losses.

twist.text: Many S&L executives committed fraud. Charles Keating alone caused $3.4 billion in losses and went to prison.

climax.text: The S&L crisis taught America that deregulating banks without supervision creates fraud, risk, and taxpayer bailouts.

punchline.text: $132 billion bailout. Deregulation without oversight created the crisis.

quiz.question: What caused the savings and loan crisis?
options: Deregulation that let S&Ls make risky investments

details.summary: The savings and loan crisis of the 1980s saw over 1,000 thrift institutions fail after deregulation allowed risky investments with government-insured deposits. The $160 billion cleanup was the costliest financial rescue before 2008.
details.whyItMatters: The S&L crisis proved that deregulation paired with government insurance guarantees creates catastrophic moral hazard. It was a dress rehearsal for the larger 2008 crisis that followed the same pattern.
takeaways: Deregulation in 1982 allowed S&Ls to invest far beyond traditional mortgages
Fraud was widespread, with executives looting their own institutions
Over 1,000 executives were criminally convicted in the aftermath

faq.question: How did deregulation cause the S&L crisis?
faq.answer: S&Ls had been restricted to safe mortgage lending. Deregulation let them invest in commercial real estate, junk bonds, and other risky assets while deposit insurance remained. This combination of risk-taking and government backing was a recipe for disaster.

faq.question: Why were more executives prosecuted in the S&L crisis than in 2008?
faq.answer: S&L fraud was often straightforward, with executives directly stealing from their institutions. The 2008 crisis involved complex legal activities like securitization that, while destructive, were technically within the law in most cases.
